chapter_theme: Kuruntokai 121 to 140: short poems in every landscape, most of them turning on one image set against one feeling; the cost of a missed tryst borne by the woman (121), evening that brings night with it (122), the laughing rainy season (126), the fish that fears the lotus after the heron (127), a king captured by a brow (129), love as a season and not a sickness (136), the maxim that work is men's life turned against going (135) and the oath that stakes a giver's honour on staying (137), with a run of gossip poems at the end (139, 140).

121.reading: The woman grants her friend that it is true: as the branch that took the miss of the black-faced langur, which leapt short on the slope, goes down with it, so for the hill man's failure to keep the tryst it is her broad soft shoulders that have turned pale.
121.nuance: The poem is about where the cost of a fault falls: the langur misjudged the leap but the branch bears it, the man failed the meeting but her shoulders show it. The opening மெய்யே concedes something the friend has said, probably that he is not to blame, and the simile answers it without disputing it.

thinai_evidence.note: hill slope, langur and the man of the hill country at a failed tryst

comparisons.tenor: the langur's face, black as if smeared with ink
her shoulders bearing the pallor for the man's missed tryst

thurai_akam.speaker: thalaivi
thurai_akam.note: the woman answers her friend after a tryst the man did not keep

122.reading: The woman says the water-lilies of the deep water, grey as the dull back of the green-legged heron, have closed now; evening has come, and it has not come alone, for it brings the night with it.
122.nuance: The closing lilies are the clock: their shut buds take the heron's colour as the light goes. The last line is the sting: evening, the hour of longing, is only the first of the hours she must get through without him.

thinai_evidence.note: the evening hour and its grief on the water

comparisons.tenor: the closed water-lily buds, dull grey as the heron's back

thurai_akam.speaker: thalaivi
thurai_akam.note: the woman in separation, at evening

123.reading: The friend says that the flowering grove of black-trunked punnai, with shade cool and thick as packed darkness beside white sand heaped like gathered moonlight, lies lonely: he still has not come, and the boats of our kin who hunt many fish are coming back.
123.nuance: Two similes make the grove a meeting place at once dark and bright. The line break sets வாரார் against வரூஉம்: the man does not come, the kinsmen do, so the time for meeting is closing. Said to the woman, perhaps for the man to hear, it presses him to come openly.

thinai_evidence.note: the shore grove, sand and fishing boats

comparisons.tenor: the dense cool shade of the grove
the heaped white sand

thurai_akam.speaker: thozhi
thurai_akam.note: the colophon names only the friend; the warning that the kin are returning reads as meant for the man too

124.reading: The friend tells the lord that if he calls harsh the great forest of omai trees, desolate as a wide town left waste after the salt-traders camped and moved on, then is the house sweet to those left in it alone?
124.nuance: She takes his own word (இன்னா) and turns it round: the abandoned camp of the simile is already a picture of the house he would leave. She does not plead; she makes the forest and the home equal in harm.

thinai_evidence.note: the man's going through the waste and the woman left alone

comparisons.tenor: the empty omai forest, like a town deserted after the salt-traders' camp
the house left alone is as harsh as the forest he dreads

thurai_akam.speaker: thozhi
thurai_akam.note: the friend answers the man who would leave

125.reading: The woman tells her friend that though her bright bangles slip and she has wasted, she is still alive; but her beauty, which outshone at festivals even the leaf-skirted women of the slope, has turned away from her along with the lord of the cool harbour where a forlorn heron, its old wing-strength gone, sits on a bent branch the waves wash.
125.nuance: The heron that can no longer fly and sits on a wave-washed branch is close to her own state, but she speaks as a girl of the slope about a man of the shore, so the condition that the heroine use only things she knows is not clear; it is left as scene (a near-miss ullurai). கண்மாறின்று, 'has turned its face away', makes her beauty a companion that has left with him.

thinai_evidence.note: the heron, the waves and the man of the harbour

126.reading: The woman tells her friend that those who went for wealth without regard for youth have not come back, and the fragrant cool rainy season, with the clustered buds of the flowering mullai the rain has fed for its bright teeth, laughs, as if asking where they are.
126.nuance: The season's laugh is mockery: the buds are white teeth and the question எவணரோ is put in the season's mouth. The first line is the charge: they did not weigh youth, which passes, against wealth, which can wait.

thinai_evidence.note: the rains and mullai in bud, the season he promised

comparisons.tenor: the clustered mullai buds as the laughing season's teeth

thurai_akam.speaker: thalaivi
thurai_akam.note: the woman, waiting through the season he named

127.reading: The friend tells the man of the town of kaanji trees and field-plots, where the kendai fish that dived when a heron struck at it now fears the bright bud of the lotus beside it, that because his one bard proved a liar, every bard there is looks like a thief to the women he has left.
127.nuance: The lotus bud is harmless, but white-tipped like a heron's beak; the fish once caught at shies from it. The friend never says the women are the fish, and the line நீ அகன்றிசினோர்க்கு lays the blame on his leaving, not on the bard.

thinai_evidence.note: fields, kaanji trees and lotus pond of the town

comparisons.tenor: the other bards, distrusted as thieves

thurai_akam.speaker: thozhi
thurai_akam.note: the friend refuses the man's bard as go-between

ullurai.tenor: the wives the man left, made wary of every bard by one deceiver

pairs.situation: the women once taken in by the man's lying bard
they now fear every bard, even the honest ones

ullurai.speaker_fit: the friend uses the heron, fish and lotus of the marutham field in a marutham poem (porul 7.27)

128.reading: The man tells his heart that, like a heron on the waves of the eastern sea that has lost its wings and longs for the rich ayirai fish of the front harbour of Thondi of Poraiyan of the sturdy chariots, it pines for one who is far away and hard to win, and that suffering is its lot.
128.nuance: The heron is on the east coast and Thondi is on the west, and the bird cannot fly: the simile measures the girl's distance by the width of the land and the lover's helplessness by the lost wings.

thinai_evidence.note: sea, heron and harbour

comparisons.tenor: the heart longing for a girl far off and hard to reach

129.reading: The man tells his comrade, the friend who gladdens boys and keeps company with poets, to listen: the small forehead gleaming beside her hair, like the fresh white moon of the eighth day rising out of the dark sea, has bound him like a newly captured elephant.
129.nuance: The eighth-day moon is a half disc, the shape of a small brow, and its rising from black water is the brow against dark hair. The poet is the Chola Kopperunchozhan, and the image of capture is a king's: he who takes elephants is himself taken like one.

thinai_evidence.note: the first sight of the girl that binds the man, told to his comrade

comparisons.tenor: her small forehead shining beside her dark hair
the man held fast by her brow

thurai_akam.speaker: thalaivan
thurai_akam.note: the man tells his comrade why he is changed

130.reading: The friend says their lover will not burrow into the earth, climb the sky or walk across the sea; if they search country by country, town by town, household by household, can he be lost?
130.nuance: The three denials close off every place but the peopled land, and the doubled words (நாட்டின் நாட்டின், ஊரின் ஊரின், குடிமுறை குடிமுறை) act out the search. The comfort lies in the certainty, not in any plan to go. Tradition makes the poet a woman who went in search of her husband; the colophon gives the words to the friend.

thinai_evidence.note: the lover gone far away and the woman left behind

131.reading: The man tells his heart that the town where she stays, she of broad shoulders lovely as swaying bamboo and large fighting eyes, lies very far over a hard road, yet the heart is as eager as a farmer with a single plough when his green field is wet and ready; and he grieves.
131.nuance: The one-plough farmer has one chance while the soil holds the rain: the simile is about timing, the urgency of a moment that will pass. The poet's name, Orerruzhavanar, comes from this line.

thinai_evidence.note: the long hard road between the man and her town

comparisons.tenor: her broad shoulders
the heart's eagerness to reach her

thurai_akam.speaker: thalaivan
thurai_akam.note: the man, far from home, to his heart

132.reading: The man asks how he can forget her, fierce in embrace, of lovely beauty, with rounded soft breasts and creeper-long hair, the dark girl who looked at him with a drooping gaze like the longing of the trembling-headed calf of a good full-uddered cow to see its mother.
132.nuance: The list of her body ends on a look, and the look is likened not to a lover's but to a calf's need for its mother: helpless dependence is what binds him. The cow and calf are herders' things in a hill love poem.

thinai_evidence.note: the man who cannot forget the girl he has met

comparisons.tenor: her drooping, longing look
her long hair, like a creeper

thurai_akam.speaker: thalaivan
thurai_akam.note: the man answers a comrade who would have him forget her

133.reading: The woman tells her friend that, like the stubble of the hill farmer's golden millet, cropped short by parrots, which puts out leaves again in heavy rain, she is still alive in the loneliness that followed his first taking of her beauty.
133.nuance: The parrots that ate the millet and the man who 'newly ate' her beauty (நலம் புதிது உண்ட) share the verb உண், so the simile carries both the loss and the survival. உரஞ் செத்தும் may mean 'though my strength is dead' or 'thinking of his firmness'; the sense of line 4 turns on it.

thinai_evidence.note: the hill farmer's millet field and parrots

comparisons.tenor: the millet heads, golden
the woman who lives on after her beauty was taken

134.reading: The woman tells her friend that the friendship joined with the man of the crossing hills, where the swift waterfall strikes the flowered swaying branch of the tall vengai on the small hill till it is bare, dashes roaring on the rocks and slides down like a snake taking the ground, would be good beyond anything if only it brought no parting.
134.nuance: The waterfall strips the vengai of its flowers and then runs away down the hill; she names only the parting, and lets the scene say the rest.

thinai_evidence.note: vengai, waterfall and hills of the man's country

comparisons.tenor: the waterfall sliding down the slope

ullurai.tenor: the man whose love has stripped the woman's bloom and who goes away

pairs.situation: his love has struck her in her bloom and left her desolate
he slips away down the hill, out of reach

ullurai.speaker_fit: the woman uses the vengai and waterfall of her own hill, things she knows (porul 7.26)

135.reading: The friend tells the woman not to cry: he himself told them that work is life to men and men are life to bright-browed women who keep the house, so he will put off his going.
135.nuance: The hero spoke both halves of the maxim; the friend leans on the second to cancel the first. If he is her life as work is his, going for work would kill what he works for.

thinai_evidence.note: the man's going for work, held back

comparisons.tenor: work as men's very life

thurai_akam.speaker: thozhi
thurai_akam.note: the friend comforts the woman who weeps at his going

136.reading: The man says people keep saying 'love, love', but love is neither a possessing spirit nor a disease; it does not grow fine and flare and subside; like the musth that comes on an elephant chewing soft fodder, it has its season, when it finds someone to look on.
136.nuance: He answers a charge, probably his comrade's, that his love is an affliction: it is a native season of the body, latent like musth, which the sight of her brings out.

thinai_evidence.note: the elephant and its fodder of the hill

comparisons.tenor: love, which rises when it finds one to look on

thurai_akam.speaker: thalaivan
thurai_akam.note: the man answers a comrade who calls his love a sickness

137.reading: The man tells his soft-natured wife that if he ever leaves her and stays away so that her good breast grows lonely, may he have many days when suppliants leave him and do not come: that is what his going would deserve.
137.nuance: The curse he takes on is the worst a giver can suffer, to be passed over by those who ask, and men usually leave home to earn the wealth to give; so he stakes the reason for going against going.

thinai_evidence.note: the man's oath against leaving

thurai_akam.speaker: thalaivan
thurai_akam.note: the man swears to his wife he will not leave

138.reading: The friend says that though the town sleeps uselessly, they do not sleep, hearing clearly the sound of the sapphire-blue flowers dropping from the lovely soft branches of the dark-clustered nochchi with leaves like peacock's feet, beside their house on the height.
138.nuance: They are awake enough to hear nochchi flowers fall, the faintest sound there is, and the sleeping town is set against the two who keep watch. Line 2 may name the hill Ezhil (அயலது ஏழில் உம்பர்), but the word division is unsure. Nothing in the poem is of the marutham fields; night, watching and the waiting for a man fit kurinji.

thinai_evidence.note: the sleepless night of waiting while the town sleeps

comparisons.tenor: the nochchi leaves, spread like a peacock's foot
the blue nochchi flowers, like sapphire

thurai_akam.speaker: thozhi
thurai_akam.note: the friend tells the man of the night watch; the colophon says only that the friend speaks

139.reading: The friend tells the man not to come to their street, for the gossip there sounds as harshly as the cry of a short-legged house hen who, when a wildcat comes to the fence at evening, cannot find where to go and calls her frightened chicks together.
139.nuance: The simile makes the street an alarmed household and quietly casts the man as the cat at the fence. அம்பல் is the first murmur of talk about secret lovers, before it becomes அலர், so the situation is kalavu and the karu of house and fence are borrowed from the town.

thinai_evidence.note: gossip about a secret love; the man told to keep away

comparisons.tenor: the harsh sound of the street's gossip

thurai_akam.speaker: thozhi
thurai_akam.note: the friend turns the man away from the street

140.reading: The woman says her lover has gone through the waste where the old male chameleon with a saw-toothed back sits and travellers take it for an omen; how did this noisy town come to know the grief she has borne here with her strength broken?
140.nuance: She has kept the grief to herself, so the town's knowing is a second injury: the gossip is about a pain she never voiced.

thinai_evidence.note: the waste he went through

comparisons.tenor: the chameleon's serrated back

links.note: Both by the poet of the paalai (Perunkadungo): the man calls the waste harsh (இன்னா, Kuruntokai 124; கடுமைய காடு, Kalittokai 6) and the woman's side answers him.
links.teaches: The same poet gives the same plea two answers: in the short poem the friend argues the house alone is as harsh as the forest, a reason for him to stay, while the long poem has the woman draw the next step, that hardship shared on the road is her only joy, so the argument from equal harm leads straight to the demand to go with him.

links.note: Both say the fragrant cool rain-season laughs with mullai buds for bright teeth (முல்லை ... இலங்கெயிறு ... நறுந்தண் கார் ... நகும்); in Kar Narpathu 14 the friend reads the laugh as proof he will come quickly, in Kuruntokai 126 the woman hears it mocking her: where are they?
links.teaches: The later poet took the older line almost word for word and reversed what it means: the same laughing season is a sign of his return to the friend who comforts and a jeer at the deserted woman, which shows that the image itself carries no fixed mood and the speaker's place in the situation decides it.

links.note: Both use the same half-line, திண்டேர்ப் பொறையன் தொண்டி: Akananuru 60 makes the girl's bangle as fine as Poraiyan's Thondi; Kuruntokai 128 makes the girl the ayirai fish of Thondi's harbour, longed for by a wingless heron on the eastern sea.
links.teaches: Poraiyan's Thondi served the love poets as a stock measure of the desirable, but they could aim it two ways: as a measure of the girl's worth that the man must win by marriage, or, set against the eastern sea, as a measure of how far out of reach she is.

links.note: Both are by Kopperunchozhan: in Kuruntokai 129 he tells his comrade, 'friend of poets', that a girl's brow has bound him like a new-caught elephant; in Purananuru 216, fasting to death, he tells doubters his poet-friend, whom he has never seen, will surely come.
links.teaches: Read together, the king's two voices turn on the same bond of male friendship: in the love poem the comrade is the one he confides his captivity to, in the death poem the friend's coming is the proof of his worth, so the paangan of akam convention is, for this poet, a role he filled with a real friendship of poets.

links.note: Both quote a saying about men's work: 'work is life to men' (வினையே ஆடவர்க்கு உயிரே, Kuruntokai 135) and 'effort, not grace, is men's wealth' (அருள் அன்று ஆக ஆள்வினை ஆடவர் பொருள், Akananuru 75); in both the man does not leave.
links.teaches: The maxim that a man's life or wealth is his work was common enough to be quoted, yet in both poems it is quoted only to be overruled: the Akananuru hero weighs it against beauty that cannot be given back, and the Kuruntokai friend completes it with its other half, that men are women's life, so the love poets used the work ethic as the premise they argue against.

links.note: Kural 1151 (the friend or the woman to the man): if you are not leaving, tell me; tell your quick return to those who will be alive then. Kuruntokai 135: the friend tells the woman he himself said men are women's life, so he will hold back.
links.teaches: The couplet states as a threat what the Kuruntokai friend leaves the man to infer from his own words: if men are the women's life, then his going kills her and any promise of a quick return is addressed to the dead, which is why the friend can be sure he will stay.

links.note: Kural 1227 (the woman) calls love a sickness that buds in the morning, opens through the day and blooms at evening; Kuruntokai 136 (the man) says love is neither a spirit nor a disease and does not swell and subside, but has its season like an elephant's musth when it finds one to look on.
links.teaches: The two agree that love keeps time but disagree on what kind of thing it is: the Kural's woman makes it a disease with a daily clock inside her, the Kuruntokai's man denies it is a sickness at all and makes it a latent season set off from outside by sight, so whether love is illness depends on whether one is waiting or seeing.

links.note: In Akananuru 279 the man leaves because men who stay at their wife's breast cannot bear to see friends in want and kin in distress; in Kuruntokai 137 the man swears that if he ever leaves his wife, may suppliants stop coming to him.
links.teaches: The same value, being the one the needy come to, drives the man out of the house in the Akananuru and binds him to it in the Kuruntokai, where losing the suppliants is the curse for leaving, so the puram duty to give could be argued on either side of the akam choice to go or stay.

links.note: Kuruntokai 140: the woman asks how the gossiping town came to know the grief she bore in silence; Kural 1180: the woman says it is not hard for the town to learn the secret of those whose eyes beat it out like a drum.
links.teaches: The Kural answers the Kuruntokai woman's question: she kept silent, but her eyes told the town, so the gossip she resents is her own grief made public by her body, not betrayal by anyone else.

source_issues: 126: line 1 (இளமை பாரார் வளநசைஇச் சென்றோர்) is flagged as not in sangamtamil.com; our text keeps it and the poem needs it, since it is the subject of வாரார் in line 2.
128: line 4 is the reading of tamilvu.org (U. V. Swaminatha Aiyar), which agrees with sangamtamil.com and replaces the base text.
132: line 1 is flagged as not in sangamtamil.com; our text keeps it, and the list of her body begins there.

138: the colophon thinai is மருதம் in the base text and குறிஞ்சி in sangamtamil.com; nothing in the poem is of the fields, and the night watch fits kurinji, which is the inferred thinai here. Line 2's division (எம்மி லயல தேழி லும்பர்) hides a possible hill name ஏழில், which therefore cannot be cited as an entity.

139: the colophon gives மருதம், but அம்பல் (the first talk about secret lovers) and the man told to keep away from the street point to kalavu; the inferred thinai is kurinji, with the house hen and fence as borrowed marutham things.

139: the simile marker ஆங்கு is split by sandhi across lines 4 and 5 (தாஅங் / கின்னா), so the marker is cited as ஆஅங்; likewise 133 (தாங்கென்) cites ஆங், 133 பொன்போற் cites போற், and 129 (பிணித்தற்றால்) cites அற்றால்.
